clue.text: What the pianist's assistant does at the pastrycook's !

definitions.text: What the pianist's assistant does at the pastrycook's !

parts.words: What the pianist's assistant does at the pastrycook's
parts.note: a page-turner flips the pianist's sheet music, and the pastrycook sells a folded pie of that name

explanation.surface: A musician's helper finds themselves doing their job in a bakery.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses run together: the pianist's assistant turns the pages over, and a pastrycook's shop sells the folded fruit pastry of the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Flipping a page is this verb phrase, and a folded pastry half filled with fruit is the matching noun.

clue.text: Thanks to the poet at the inn

parts.note: ta is informal British for thank you
a bard is a poet, and the Bard is Shakespeare

explanation.surface: Gratitude is owed to a poet drinking at a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' and 'at' only link the pieces and the definition; the Tabard in Southwark is the inn where Chaucer's pilgrims gather.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tabard was the Southwark hostelry where Chaucer's Canterbury pilgrims met, so a famous inn.

clue.text: It takes more than one kingdom to produce a genuine manuscript

parts.note: real means genuine or authentic

explanation.surface: It needs several nations to produce one authentic ancient text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It takes' and 'to produce' only link; 'more than one kingdom' asks for a plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Domains ruled by monarchs, plural, as the definition asks for several.

clue.text: " For the pretty little flower and the great" (Gilbert)

definitions.text: " For the pretty little flower and the great" (Gilbert)

parts.words: For the pretty little flower and the great
parts.note: a line of W. S. Gilbert's lyrics pairing a small bloom with a mighty tree, its last words left blank

explanation.surface: A line of W. S. Gilbert verse with its final words missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the blank in Gilbert's line: the little flower is contrasted with the great forest giant grown from an acorn.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilbert contrasts a small bloom with a large broadleaf tree that grows from acorns.

clue.text: Not that they're used for the first course !

definitions.text: Not that they're used for the first course !

parts.words: Not that they're used for the first course
parts.note: the French word for the starter is borrowed for these serving vessels, yet they are not used for the opening course

explanation.surface: A note that certain tableware is never brought out with the starters.
explanation.walkthrough: The French name means 'entrance', and Americans use it for the main course, but in the classic British dinner the entrée came after the fish, not first.
explanation.definitionFit: Covered serving vessels for the entrée, the dish served between fish and roast in a formal dinner.

clue.text: Stuffy plays for French cooks ?

parts.note: light comic plays share a name with the French cook's word for forcemeat stuffing

explanation.surface: Dull theatre aimed at chefs from France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuffy' does not mean dull: the French farce is a stuffing, the source of the name for knockabout comedy, so these plays are literally stuffing for cooks.
explanation.definitionFit: Broad comedies of improbable situations take their name from the French culinary term for forcemeat.

clue.text: "Oh! what a thousand pities then That Adam was not-" (Hood)

definitions.text: "Oh! what a thousand pities then That Adam was not-" (Hood)

parts.words: Oh! what a thousand pities then That Adam was not
parts.note: Thomas Hood's couplet ends with a word built on the name of the first man, meaning unyielding

explanation.surface: A Thomas Hood couplet regretting something about Adam, its last word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Hood's pun extends the name in the line: had Adam been unbending, he would have resisted the apple.
explanation.definitionFit: Unshakeably firm and refusing to give way, a word that happens to begin with the first man's name.

clue.text: A drink may show which way the wind's blowing !

definitions.text: A drink may show which way the wind's blowing !

parts.words: A drink may show which way the wind's blowing
parts.note: a mixed drink shares a name with the tail of a rooster, as on a weathervane

explanation.surface: A tipple reveals how the mood is shifting.
explanation.walkthrough: A weathercock's tail points the wind's direction, and the same two words name a mixed drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A mixed alcoholic drink, and also the rear plumage of a rooster such as the one on a weathervane.

clue.text: Container for the surgeon's triumph ?

parts.note: a surgeon's prize patient is a case worth showing off, and a glass display cabinet holds exhibits

explanation.surface: A box to hold a doctor's greatest success.
explanation.walkthrough: A surgeon's triumph is a 'show case', a patient fit to exhibit; the hyphenated word is a glass display cabinet.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass-fronted cabinet for displaying exhibits, read as the patient a surgeon proudly exhibits.

clue.text: And the rough, male kiss of " (Brooke)

definitions.text: And the rough, male kiss of

parts.words: And the rough, male kiss of
parts.note: a line from Rupert Brooke's poem The Great Lover, listing the things he loved, with its last word left blank

explanation.surface: A quotation from Rupert Brooke with its final word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in Brooke's line from The Great Lover: the coarse wool bedcovers are what give the rough, male kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet names woollen bedcovers as the thing whose coarse touch feels like a rough, manly kiss.

clue.text: Knightly attendant discovered in partisan chorus

indicators.note: discovered means uncovered, found lying inside the following words partisan chorus

explanation.surface: A knight's servant turns up among a crowd of supporters singing together.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the join of partiSAN CHOrus.
explanation.definitionFit: Sancho Panza is the squire who serves Don Quixote, the would-be knight errant.

clue.text: Sensational outcome of Democrat mail

indicators.note: the outcome is what results when the words Democrat and mail are worked over into a new order

explanation.surface: Political post produces a lurid result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outcome of' rearranges DEMOCRAT and MAIL together.
explanation.definitionFit: Exaggerated and overemotional, like the stage melodrama, is what sensational means.

clue.text: Conscience having a second bite ?

parts.note: the word comes from Latin for biting again, as guilt gnaws at a person a second time

explanation.surface: A guilty conscience returns to nag at someone again.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin remordere means to bite again, the old 'agenbite of inwit': guilt that gnaws a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: Regret and guilt over a wrong are what an uneasy conscience inflicts, from the Latin for re-biting.

clue.text: Scale it at a stretch ?

indicators.note: stretched letters are pulled out of shape, so the words scale it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A climber is told to tackle a wall in one long go.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: 'at a stretch' rearranges SCALEIT, and something you can stretch has this quality.
explanation.definitionFit: A material that can be pulled out and spring back is stretchy, which is what the whole clue describes.

clue.text: Chance of a drop in currency

definitions.text: Chance of a drop in currency

parts.words: Chance of a drop in currency
parts.note: reads like a fall in the exchange rate, but describes the gamble of a tossed coin landing one face up

explanation.surface: A financial forecast warns the pound might fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop in currency' sounds like devaluation; it is a coin dropped after being tossed, and which face lands up is pure chance.
explanation.definitionFit: Tossing a coin and calling which face will land up is the classic way of leaving a decision to luck.

clue.text: Columnists' shelters ?

parts.note: not newspaper writers but things with columns: roofed porches held up by pillars

explanation.surface: Places where newspaper writers take cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Columnists' looks like journalists; here it is whatever is made of columns, roofed porches on pillars.
explanation.definitionFit: Roofed porches supported by columns at the entrance to a building give shelter.

clue.text: It's recognized in the pharmacopoeia

parts.note: in pharmacy a drug listed in the authorised book of medicines is described by this word

explanation.surface: A drug has been formally approved for use.
explanation.walkthrough: In pharmacy the word describes a drug listed in the authorised pharmacopoeia; more generally anything authorised is so described.
explanation.definitionFit: Authorised and formally recognised, as a drug listed in the standard pharmacopoeia is.

clue.text: The High, W.1 ?

definitions.meaning: the High is the main thoroughfare of the university city of Oxford
W1 is the London postcode district holding the famous shopping street named after Oxford

explanation.walkthrough: THE HIGH is the main street of Oxford; London's W1 postal district contains the busiest shopping road in Britain, which bears Oxford's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are thoroughfares tied to the university city: its own High Street, and the London shopping road named after it.

clue.text: Reproved in a Scotch book bound in crimson

indicators.note: a book bound in a colour is wrapped in it, so the book goes inside the word for crimson

parts.note: crimson is a shade of red
buke is the Scots word for book

explanation.surface: Someone is scolded within a red-covered Scottish volume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' only links; Scots spells book with a U and a final E, and 'bound in' puts it inside the colour, as a volume sits in its cover.
explanation.definitionFit: Scolded or reprimanded, which is what reproved means.

clue.text: Orders put together in three quarters

indicators.note: in places the phrase for put together inside the letters for the three quarters

parts.note: E, N and S are three of the four compass points, called quarters
join means put together

explanation.surface: Commands assembled from three fourths of a whole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'three quarters' looks like a fraction; it is three compass quarters, E, N and S, around JOIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Directs or commands, as orders does as a verb.

clue.text: Can one have too much of music?

definitions.text: Can one have too much of music?

parts.words: Can one have too much of music
parts.note: the Italian score marking meaning excessively is what music says for too much

explanation.surface: A question whether it is possible to overdo music.
explanation.walkthrough: In score markings such as allegro ma non troppo, the Italian word means 'too much', so music can indeed have it.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian for excessively, used in tempo markings like non troppo, meaning not overdone.

clue.text: The sign for spit-and-polish

parts.note: military slang for fussy spit-and-polish is bull, and a zodiac sign is the Bull

explanation.surface: A badge or emblem for smartness on the parade ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Spit-and-polish is 'bull' in army slang, and the zodiac sign of the Bull has this Latin name.
explanation.definitionFit: The zodiac sign represented by a bull, and bull is soldiers' slang for excessive smartening up.

clue.text: It's rigged in legerdemain

parts.note: a sleight-of-hand swindle uses three small cups and a pea, and the cup gives the con its name

explanation.surface: Sleight of hand tricks are fixed in advance.
explanation.walkthrough: The old three-cup and pea con trick is named after the sewing cap used as the cup plus 'rig', so that cap is what gets 'rigged' in the sleight of hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A seamstress's finger cap was the cup used in the thimblerig shell game, the hustler's sleight of hand.

clue.text: Big brother at a hundred and one makes for the island

parts.note: at British schools the elder of two brothers is called Major, the younger Minor
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
A is one, as in the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An elder sibling turning a hundred and one heads off to an island.
explanation.walkthrough: British public schools tell brothers apart as Smith major (elder) and Smith minor (younger); 'and' and 'makes for' only link.
explanation.definitionFit: Majorca is the largest of the Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean.

clue.text: Cracks agreeable to a miser

parts.note: narrow gaps share a name with the clinking sound and slang for coins that a hoarder loves

explanation.surface: Gaps that a skinflint is pleased to see.
explanation.walkthrough: Narrow cracks have the same name as coins, called after their clink, which is the sound a miser loves.
explanation.definitionFit: Narrow openings or slits, and also slang for coins from the clinking noise money makes.

clue.text: Canine beautician with night-club potential

parts.note: a dog groomer who plucks dead hair from a coat shares a title with a striptease artiste

explanation.surface: A dog groomer who might also make it in cabaret.
explanation.walkthrough: Groomers 'strip' a wire-haired dog's dead coat by hand; in a night-club the same title belongs to a striptease dancer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hand-plucking a terrier's coat is called stripping, and an undressing performer in a club bears the same title.

clue.text: Greenery for the young Cleopatra

parts.note: in Shakespeare's play Cleopatra calls her youth her days when she was green in judgment

explanation.surface: Fresh vegetation given to the Egyptian queen when she was a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Cleopatra speaks of 'My salad days, when I was green in judgment', so her youthful greenery is this dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Dishes of raw green leaves, and Cleopatra's phrase for her inexperienced youth.

clue.text: They may be closed in declaring the road open

definitions.text: They may be closed in declaring the road open

parts.words: They may be closed in declaring the road open
parts.note: at an opening ceremony a dignitary cuts a ribbon, the two blades snapping shut on it

explanation.surface: A paradox: something shut so that a new road can be opened.
explanation.walkthrough: The paradox resolves at a ribbon-cutting: the blades close to cut the tape that opens the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutting tool of two pivoted blades, used by dignitaries to snip the ribbon at openings.
